# Saddle, stirrups and horseshoes (`stirrup_saddle`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by cavalry_chariot, bloomery_iron
- Core idea: A treed saddle spreads the rider's weight over the horse's back; paired stirrups give the rider a firm stance to mount, stand, shoot and strike without being unseated; nailed iron shoes protect hooves on hard and wet ground. Together they let riders travel far and fight from the saddle. In 1490 all three are familiar in Florence; their use elsewhere varies with riding traditions and local conditions.
- Pitfalls:
  - Repeating Lynn White's thesis that the stirrup created mounted shock combat and feudalism; most historians reject it
  - Thinking riders without stirrups could not fight on horseback; Roman four-horned saddles held riders very well
  - Shoeing an unshod horse badly; misplaced nails lame it
- History: india: 2nd c. BC – toe stirrups on Sanchi reliefs; china: c. 302 AD – single mounting stirrup on a Changsha tomb figure; paired stirrups by c. 322 AD (Nanjing) and 415 (Feng Sufu tomb); east_asia: 5th c. – stirrups in Korea (Goguryeo) and Japan; europe: late 6th c. – Avars bring stirrups; c. 600 Strategikon recommends them; nailed horseshoes common by the 10th c.; rome: 1st c. BC onward – four-horned saddle
- Read:
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
  - Bernard S. Bachrach, Charles Martel, Mounted Shock Combat, the Stirrup, and Feudalism, Studies in Medieval and Renaissance History 7 (1970)
